name: Lumecca IPL

lead: Lumecca is an intense pulsed light (IPL) device from InMode, used in clinics to fade brown spots, freckles and facial redness for a more even complexion. IPL is not a laser; it uses broad-spectrum flashes rather than a single wavelength.

Filters select which targets absorb the light, melanin in pigment or hemoglobin in small vessels, and the heat breaks up pigment or closes small vessels, with surface cooling to protect skin. Studies naming Lumecca are small: 38 volunteers had dilated facial vessel response measured after three sessions, and a 20-patient study assessed redness reduction in rosacea after polychromatic light treatments.

paras: Treatment is done in a clinic, typically as a short series of sessions weeks apart. Spots often darken before flaking away. IPL is generally described as having little downtime.

IPL complications can include hyperpigmentation, especially on darker skin, and one manufacturer states IPL suits light to medium skin tones. Photosensitising drugs and damaged skin are contraindications. It is a professional device.

angle.text: Lumecca flashes broad-spectrum light that targets pigment and redness, fading sun spots, freckles and vessels for a more even facial tone. It is an IPL rather than a laser, and supporting studies are small, though IPL is an established category.

lead: Lumecca is a high-intensity intense pulsed light (IPL) device made by InMode, used in clinics for facial pigment and redness.[1] Patients seek it to fade brown sun spots and freckles, reduce facial redness and visible thread veins, and even out skin tone so the complexion looks clearer. IPL is not a laser: a xenon flashlamp emits broad-spectrum, non-coherent light, and filters select which light-absorbing targets (melanin or haemoglobin) are heated.[2]

Published research naming Lumecca is limited to small studies. A study of 38 volunteers used three Lumecca IPL sessions and measured the response of dilated facial blood vessels with quantitative methods,[1] and a 20-patient study of rosacea used three Lumecca treatments at 21-day intervals and reported a mean 61 percent fall in a clinician erythema score.[3][4] A 2025 registered trial compares IPL, an anti-redness cosmetic and their combination in rosacea.[5]

paras: IPL devices use a flashlamp that emits roughly 400 to 1200 nm, with filters that cut off shorter and longer wavelengths. Melanin, haemoglobin and water absorb the light and heat, and cooling protects the skin surface.[2] IPL was invented by Shimon Eckhouse in 1992, with US clearances for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.[2]

Reference sources list photorejuvenation, pigmentation, sun damage, thread veins, rosacea, acne and melasma among IPL uses.[2] The Lumecca-specific study found that three treatments allowed vessel response to be quantified in 38 volunteers.[1] The rosacea study authors describe IPL as a recognised treatment for erythema and telangiectasia and emphasise combining clinical assessment with imaging analysis.[3]

In the 2024 study, 38 volunteers received three IPL treatments with Lumecca, and vessel response was measured with mexametry, hyperspectral imaging and directional reflectance. Mexametry showed no statistically significant change in haemoglobin content, hyperspectral imaging showed a significant post-treatment increase in skin reflectance at 580 nm, and directional reflectance showed significant increases in the 400 to 540 nm and 480 to 600 nm ranges. The authors concluded that three IPL sessions appear adequate for a clinically satisfactory reduction in facial vascular changes and that hyperspectral imaging was an effective quantitative method.[1][4]

In the 2025 rosacea study, 20 patients received three Lumecca treatments (515 to 1200 nm) at 21-day intervals. Erythema was scored on the Clinician Erythema Assessment scale and skin texture was analysed with grey level co-occurrence matrix measures. All patients improved: the mean erythema score fell by 61.11 percent, texture contrast fell by about 17 percent, homogeneity rose by 4 to 5 percent, and effects lasted at least three months.[3][4] Neither study had a control group in the data summarised here.

Reference sources note that complications such as hyperpigmentation can occur, that photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are contraindications, and that one manufacturer advises IPL and laser devices only for light to medium skin tones.[2]

A 38-volunteer study used three Lumecca IPL treatments to evaluate quantitative methods for assessing dilated facial vessels.[1] A 20-patient study assessed rosacea erythema after three polychromatic light treatments, with a mean 61 percent fall in the clinician erythema score and effects lasting at least three months.[3] NCT07729540, a 60-participant trial started in 2025, compares IPL, an anti-redness dermocosmetic and both together in rosacea.[5] All are small, and results of the registered trial are not available in the registry entry cited here.

timeline.event: Shimon Eckhouse invents intense pulsed light.[2]
First US clearance for IPL on vascular lesions.[2]
US clearance for IPL hair removal.[2]
Study of 38 volunteers uses Lumecca to compare quantitative methods for assessing facial vessels.[1]
Twenty-patient Lumecca rosacea study reports erythema reduction; registered IPL rosacea trial begins.[3][5]
